One Nation candidate for Murray Plains says climate change isn't real
One Nation candidate for Murray Plains Garner Smith has told the ABC he doesn't believe in the science behind climate change.
Asked on ABC Central Victoria Breakfast this morning whether he accepted the consensus of the world's leading climate scientists, he said: "No, I don't actually.

"In fact, as far as I'm concerned, climate change has become nothing more than a mechanism that transfers money and power from the many to the few," he said. "I think there'd be a lot of people out there that'd be absolutely relieved to hear somebody say that."
"In fact, as far as I'm concerned, climate change has become nothing more than a mechanism that transfers money and power from the many to the few," he said.
"I think there'd be a lot of people out there that'd be absolutely relieved to hear somebody say that."
The former mayor for Gannawarra Shire in north Victoria and Nationals Candidate said while he wasn't a scientist, he studied "all the sciences" in high school.
"Got 100 per cent in physics actually when I did my HSC in high school … So I would consider myself to be as scientifically minded as anybody," he said.
Smith also reiterated One Nation's commitment to scrap the proposed VNI West electricity transmission project and said he was not particularly supportive of wind or solar developments.

"We're really after making sure that renewable projects are considered the right way. Right now they've been pushed through by the Labor government," he said. "I would mount the argument that it would be net negative benefit for the local communities because we'll probably see farmers stop farming."

Carroll asked about targeting Greens in Melbourne's west

Earlier, we told you about an issue in Melbourne's west where it appears Labor volunteers are handing out flyers in Point Cook that incorrectly suggest the Greens aren't making preference recommendations this election.
The Greens are only running an open ticket in some seats due to a preference stoush with Labor.
Premier Ben Carroll doesn't answer three questions about whether they're doing something dodgy with the flyer.

"Our Labor volunteers are out there every single day telling Victorians what a risk a Liberal-One Nation coalition is," he says. "We're making sure every Victorian, no matter where their community is, knows you must put Labor number 1."

Carroll in Allan territory
It's been three-and-a-half months since Jacinta Allan was pushed from the Labor party leadership and Ben Carroll replaced her as premier.
A journalist at today's press conferences raises the fact that Ben Carroll is in Jacinta Allan's hometown.
Allan isn't standing for election, and her seat of Bendigo East is under threat from the Nationals and One Nation.
Carroll says this isn't his first visit to Bendigo and that he's "been in the local pubs" with the two Labor candidates for the two Bendigo seats ahead of the election.
"Every seat we're fighting for," he says. "We have transformed Bendigo for the better."
"Every seat we're fighting for," he says.
"We have transformed Bendigo for the better."
Labor announces free dental check-ups at kinders and childcare
The Ben Carroll election bus has pulled up at an early learning centre in Bendigo.
He's announcing that Smile Squad — a free, mobile oral health and dental check-up van that visits Victorian state schools — will be expanded to kindergartens and day care.
"This is a policy about giving people the health care they need but it's also a structural cost-of-living measure as well," Carroll says.
Health Minister Ingrid Stitt says statistics show around half of 4- and 5-year-olds have got preventable tooth decay.
"The earlier we start, the better," she says.
"Being able to expand Smile Squad into our kindergarten and long day-care programs is going to be a game changer for turning around some of the more worrying statistics."
Seats in focus: Preston

Preston is set in the heart of Labor's northern suburbs heartlands. It remains deeply multicultural like the rest of the outer north but has become increasingly gentrified and well-educated like the inner north.

Bell Street, which serves as the seat's southern border, is informally known as the "Quinoa Curtain", below which the Greens have traditionally performed better compared to Labor in the north. That split has gradually broken down at the state level in part due to a reversal of Liberal preferencing decisions against the Greens and Labor's declining reputation among their multicultural core.

This was an extraordinarily complex seat to resolve in the 2022 election, when Labor's vote fell sharply to 37.6 per cent, but the next three candidates all polled in the teens. Independent Gaetano Greco, who ran a campaign opposing the redevelopment of the Preston Market, was excluded first and his preferences largely went to the Greens. If he instead outlasted the Liberals there is a chance he would have won the seat. But instead the Liberals made it one more round before being excluded and two-thirds of their preferences flowed to the Greens, leaving Labor only narrowly holding Preston.
Greco passed away in 2025 and no equally prominent independent has emerged, leaving the Greens as the most likely challenger to Labor here.

More how-to-vote cards targeting Greens voters
We covered a little earlier today a case where how-to-vote cards handed out by a Prahran independent candidate mimicked the style of Greens how-to-vote cards.
Across town in Point Cook, it appears Labor is also targeting Greens voters.

A handout states the Greens "aren't recommending preferences in the election". It then suggests to preference Labor second.
The handout is authorised by Labor state secretary Steve Staikos.
Wilson says big lines at early voting booths a symptom of angry voters
Figures from the Victorian Electoral Commission show 211,461 people turned up to vote at early voting centres yesterday.
Wilson said it was a sign that voters wanted a change in government.
"I think we saw big lines yesterday because Victorians have had enough of a corrupt government, a government that has let them down over the past 12 years," she said.
She also had a crack at revelations about conduct on government Big Build sites following revelations from the royal commission yesterday.
We heard from witness Joel Leavitt that a catering bill for souvlakis for construction workers at the Hurstbridge rail line job came in at $9,000 but was inflated to $20,000.
Text messages accompanying the invoice suggested that two CFMEU health and safety representatives pocketed $5,000, one of whom was Leavitt.

"We're listening to stories about souvlakis on Big Build sites, that means there hasn't been funding going into our police force, into our schools," she said. "So I'm not surprised that Victorians are out. They're out to change the government."
"We're listening to stories about souvlakis on Big Build sites, that means there hasn't been funding going into our police force, into our schools," she said.
"So I'm not surprised that Victorians are out. They're out to change the government."
Key Event
Jess Wilson says natural gas will be a Coalition priority
Opposition leader Jess Wilson says looking into developing Victorian natural gas exploration will be one of her first priorities if elected premier.

"I'm focused on how we get Victorian gas out of the ground for Victorians," Wilson said. "It will take time to get that gas out of the ground but we've seen a Labor government not doing it for more than a decade. "I've said I want to see expressions-of-interest to start that exploration on my desk, if I'm elected premier, within 60 days."
"I'm focused on how we get Victorian gas out of the ground for Victorians," Wilson said.
"It will take time to get that gas out of the ground but we've seen a Labor government not doing it for more than a decade.
"I've said I want to see expressions-of-interest to start that exploration on my desk, if I'm elected premier, within 60 days."
She said there would be no changes to fracking laws under a Coalition government.
The federal government is currently fighting to pass its own legislation to build a natural gas reserve to protect against shortfalls.
Labor's domestic gas reservation scheme would require natural gas producers to reserve 20 per cent of their product for the domestic market.
The government has yet to secure support from either the Coalition or Greens to pass the gas reservation scheme through the upper house.
Wilson said the matter was for her federal colleagues to discuss, and said she remains focused on Victorians.
Victorian business owner says taxes making it tough
Business owner Brett said the increase in government charges had made it difficult to survive.
"Land tax, payroll tax, it's nearly doubled in the last two years, the last 12 months," he said.
It's a point that the major parties have actually found common ground on.
Labor and the Coalition have not pledged to roll back land tax progressively to 2023 levels.
The Coalition has promised further cuts by raising the payroll tax threshold to $1.2 million.
Opposition leader Jess Wilson continues her business push
The Liberal campaign bus, dubbed the Jess Express, rolls on today with a stop at surfacing business RubberTough Industries in Warragul.
The Coalition has made it very clear where their policies are directed, stopping at yet another small business after a stop at a food producer Cooee Foods in Mordialloc yesterday.
Before she spoke, business owner Brett spoke about the impact of increased payroll and land taxes on his business, both policies the Coalition has pledged to target.
Brett also said he was looking forward to the Coalition delivering on their healthcare promises.
"I've lived here for over 60 years, and we've been waiting for a hospital for the last 10 or 12. Wayne [Farnham] has promised that, otherwise he's unemployed," he said. "It's well overdue."

"It's well overdue."
VEC says accessibility a 'key consideration' when choosing voting centres
Yesterday, the election blog reported local concerns about accessibility issues at the Silva Drive Community Centre in Wodonga.
It is one of two early voting centres in the town.
Volunteers told the ABC there have been concerns about limited parking and how people with physical disabilities could access the centre.

People handing out how-to-vote cards also say they witnessed a voter fall over a crack in the concrete and injure themselves when heading into the vote yesterday. There are also no clear footpaths along the street to the centre,
"We are aware a voter fell outside a voting centre in Wodonga [yesterday], and was assisted by Victoria Election Commission staff," a VEC spokesperson said
The VEC says it spends more than a year planning and scouting out venues for state elections.
"Accessibility is a key consideration of our assessment when we select voting centres, along with availability, parking and public transport," the spokesperson said.
"However, we don't own the buildings or the public land surrounding a voting centre.
"With these limitations, it may not be realistic for every voting centre to be fully accessible, but our goal is for every voter to have a fully accessible voting option available to them."

The VEC spokesperson also says that, along with early voting and voting on polling day, other accessible options include postal voting and telephone-assisted voting, as well as assisted wheelchair-access voting centres in Wodonga.
Regional Victoria brings a decade of frustration to state election
Regional Victoria is politically angry.
Angry at Labor for under investment during its 12 years of government.
Angry at the Liberals and Nationals for promising so much every election and failing to form government.
Angry at crumbling roads, potholes, incomplete hospitals, the fight over funding for its beloved CFA and yes, angry that funding is always promised for a sports stadium that never arrives.
It is little wonder polls have shown a big rise in support for One Nation.

Those words are from the ABC's Warwick Long, who penned an analysis this morning describing the years of frustration that regional Victorians have felt, and the seismic impact it could have on the election.

Seats in focus: Prahran

Prahran has changed hands many times over its long history, being one of the most consistently marginal seats in the state. Although it has somewhat settled as a progressive-leaning seat in the 21st century, it has still been represented by all three of Labor, the Liberals and the Greens.

The seat first became a genuine three-party contest in 2014. At that election the Greens grew their primary vote by five percentage points and were able to overtake Labor into second place, using their preferences to narrowly win the seat from the Liberals.

The successful Greens candidate Sam Hibbins held the seat with increasingly healthy margins at the following two elections, eventually reaching first place on the primary vote in 2022. He resigned in late 2024 after admitting to having an affair with one of his staff.

Labor opted not to run in the ensuing by-election and the Liberal Party narrowly regained the seat from the Greens. This was partially due to low turnout and unfavourable preference recommendations from other candidates including former Labor MP for the seat Tony Lupton, who was running as an independent.
With Labor returning to the contest, the Greens will be hoping to regain Prahran in 2026.
Key Event
Independent how-to-vote cards appear to copy Greens
The how-to-vote cards being handed out by some independent candidates around the state have raised some eyebrows.
In the Prahran electorate, where the Greens are expected to compete strongly, independent candidate Tosh-Jake Finnigan is also running.
Finnigan's how-to-vote cards seem to mimic Greens how-to-vote cards extremely closely.
However, unlike the Greens how-to-vote card, Finnigan is preferencing Greens last and Labor second-to-last.
A former Labor operative, Finnigan blew the whistle on Victorian Labor's redshirts scheme which saw the party use electoral staff to campaign for the 2014 election, costing the taxpayer $388,000.
They also recent served as a Colac Otway Shire councillor.
The ABC has reached out to Finnigan and the VEC for comment.
Seats in focus: Lara

Lara was first contested at the 2002 state election by Peter Loney, the MP for Geelong North since 1992, whose seat was being abolished. He served as Lara’s MP for just one term before facing a preselection challenge by Legislative Council member John Eren, who was set to be without a seat after the Bracks government’s reforms to the upper house. Loney decided to retire, clearing the path for Eren’s election.

Eren served in cabinet during the first term of the Andrews government but was dropped after Labor’s landslide 2018 victory. He retired in 2022 and was succeeded by Ella George, who retained the seat with a slightly reduced margin of 15.9 per cent.
Key Event
Liberals hand out Labor fidget spinners
Close followers of our politics blog will likely know that the Liberal Party likes handing out political merchandise to journalists travelling on its campaign bus (dubbed the "Jess Express").
Last week, we saw "Wake up Ben" eye masks, then pen holders in the shape of Labor’s controversial machete bins.
Today, journalists were given bright red fidget spinners emblazoned with the words "Labor spin".
"Because everything that comes out of their mouth is just spin," Opposition leader Jess Wilson told reporters as she handed out the toys.
When prompted on what she considered to be examples of Labor spin, she said the party’s claims that the Coalition would make $40 billion worth of cuts and "Americanise" the health care system.
"I mean, Ben Carroll can’t even say the two former premiers names," Wilson said, a reference to one of their exchanges during Tuesday night's leaders debate on News24.
The Jess Express is back on the road today, heading to Victoria’s east. It remains to be seen whether the fidget spinners will come in handy for reporters looking to pass the time during the journey.

Key Event
Family First Victoria disendorses Bendigo West candidate
In case you missed this news last night, Family First Victoria disendorsed its Victorian election candidate for Bendigo West over "unbecoming and unacceptable" online content and language.
Christos Harisopoulos was linked to an account on blogging website Substack, where his name is attached to several articles attacking political parties and politicians.

One post claims Labor and the Liberals had "sold 25 per cent of our land to the community party of China", and are "importing replacements" who will vote for their "traitorous politicians without question".

Family First national director Lyle Shelton told the ABC on Wednesday afternoon that Harisopoulos had been disendorsed by the party, following the identification of online content and language he was linked to.
"We are a small party with limited resources. We regret that this material was not picked up in the vetting process," Shelton said.
